# Gap analysis

The exams were read item by item. Each item was broken into the concepts a student must already hold to answer it. A gap is a concept that an item depends on but that no item tests on its own, so a course built only from the exam questions would never teach it.

## Lessons added to fill gaps (7)

These prepare for no exam item directly. Later lessons and exam items depend on them.

| Lesson | Topic | Why it was added |
|---|---|---|
| 1.2 | **Measured numbers**: Units and significant figures | Not tested as an item of its own, but the Exam 1 rubric deducts for units and significant figures, Exam 1 Q9 needs mL → L, and Exam 3 needs pm → cm and Å → m. |
| 1.3 | **Names and formulas**: Ions and compounds | Exam 1 names compounds without always giving a formula (Q1 aluminum oxide, Q6 aluminum chloride, Q8 iron(III) oxide, Q12 sodium carbonate and calcium chloride), and every ionic equation depends on knowing each ion’s charge. |
| 1.4 | **The mole**: Counting by weighing | Every calculation on Exam 1 from Q2 to Q9 starts with grams → moles. The exam prints the molar masses, but a student still has to know what they mean and which one to use. |
| 2.4 | **Enthalpy**: Heat of reaction | Exam 2 jumps straight to Hess’s law and enthalpies of formation. Both rest on three ideas taught here and tested nowhere on their own: what ΔH is, that it scales with the coefficients, and that it changes sign when the equation is reversed. |
| 2.11 | **The pull of the nucleus**: Coulomb’s law and shielding | Never asked directly, but it is the reason behind every periodic-trend item on Exam 2 (Q7, Q8, Q14, Q15, Q19) and behind where the peaks sit in a photoelectron spectrum. Without it the trends are a list to memorise. |
| 3.1 | **Why atoms bond**: Ionic, covalent and metallic | Exam 3 opens with Lewis structures, but every polarity and intermolecular-force item (Q1, Q4, Q12 to Q15, Q19) needs bond polarity first, and Q19 needs the idea of an ionic solid dissolving. None of this is tested on its own. |
| 3.12 | **Solids**: Crystals and unit cells | Exam 3 is titled “…Intermolecular Forces & Solids” and its reference sheet gives edge-length formulas, but nothing gives the number of atoms in each cell. Q16 and Q17 cannot be started without it. |

## Material added inside examined lessons (23)

| Lesson | Topic | What was added and why |
|---|---|---|
| 1.5 | **Balanced equations** | Exam 1 prints its equations already balanced for the calculations, but Q12 to Q14 need students to write and balance the molecular equation themselves before splitting it into ions. |
| 1.9 | **Solutions** | Dilution (M₁V₁ = M₂V₂) is not on Exam 1 but is the natural next question once molarity is known, and it is needed to prepare any solution used in the laboratory. |
| 1.10 | **What dissolves** | Weak electrolytes are not tested on Exam 1, but without them students cannot explain why a weak acid is written as a molecule in an ionic equation (lesson 1.12). |
| 1.12 | **Acids and bases** | Exam 1 uses only strong acids and bases. Weak acids and titration are added so that students do not conclude every acid–base net ionic equation is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, and so that molarity is put to its main laboratory use. |
| 2.1 | **System and surroundings** | Exam 2 asks only for the signs of q and w, but the signs mean nothing without the first law that ties them together. State functions are needed later for Hess’s law. |
| 2.3 | **Calorimetry** | The same method with a reaction in the cup gives the heat of the reaction: q(reaction) = −q(solution). That link, used in the next lesson, is not on Exam 2 but is how every ΔH in the tables was measured. |
| 2.6 | **Enthalpies of formation** | The exam’s table leaves O₂ out without comment; students need to know why its value is zero. |
| 2.8 | **The hydrogen atom** | The equation sheet writes the two levels as n₂ and n₁ without saying which is which. Reading it as final and initial makes the sign of ΔE tell you absorption from emission. |
| 2.9 | **Orbitals** | Exam 2 Q18 asks for all four quantum numbers of one electron. That cannot be done by rule alone; students need to know what each number means and which values are allowed. |
| 2.10 | **Electron configurations** | The Cr and Cu exceptions and the configurations of ions are not on Exam 2, but ion configurations are needed for ionic radius (2.13) and for bonding in Part 3. |
| 2.13 | **Size** | Isoelectronic ions are not on Exam 2 but are the standard next question after “compare O²⁻ and S²⁻”, and the reasoning is the same. |
| 2.14 | **Losing electrons** | Electronegativity is not on Exam 2, but Exam 3 uses it from the first question (bond polarity, molecular polarity, hydrogen bonding). It belongs with the other trends. |
| 3.3 | **Formal charge and resonance** | The reference sheet gives the formal-charge formula, but the N₂O₄ in Q1 also needs resonance, which the exam never names. Resonance is also why NO₂⁻, CO₃²⁻ and SO₂ in Q5 and Q9 count as three electron domains. |
| 3.7 | **Hybrid orbitals** | This course tests sp³d and sp³d² (Q5, Q8, Q9, Q20). The current AP Chemistry course description examines only sp, sp² and sp³, so students who also sit the AP exam should know the longer list is a course requirement, not an AP one. |
| 3.8 | **Sigma and pi bonds** | Q6 and Q7 show a large drawn molecule and ask for one kind of bond. Reading such a drawing, and counting only what is asked, is a skill the exam assumes and nothing before it teaches. |
| 3.10 | **Forces between molecules** | Ion–dipole forces are the answer to Q19 but are easy to leave out of a list that stops at hydrogen bonding. |
| 3.11 | **Boiling points** | Vapour pressure and solubility are not on Exam 3, but they are the same reasoning applied to different properties and are needed for any further work on liquids and solutions. |
| 4.1 | **Collisions** | The Final starts with rate calculations. Its Q1 lists temperature, surface area, catalyst and concentration as answer choices, and nothing earlier in the course explains why any of them matters. |
| 4.2 | **Measuring rate** | Initial rate is the quantity used in the method of initial rates (4.4); the Final uses the idea without defining it. |
| 4.5 | **First-order reactions** | These items need ln and eˣ, which the course has not used before. A line on what they are and how they undo each other is included so the mathematics does not hide the chemistry. |
| 4.6 | **Zero and second order** | Zero-order reactions are asked about (Q17) but their integrated law and half-life are never used in a calculation; they are given here so the set of three is complete. |
| 4.7 | **Temperature** | Q1 is a kinetic-energy distribution and Q18 mentions “frequency factors”. Both come from the Arrhenius picture, which the Final assumes. Kelvin is introduced here because the course has no gases unit to introduce it. |
| 4.9 | **Mechanisms** | Q11 and Q19 both put a fast reversible step before the slow one. Solving them needs the idea that forward and reverse rates balance, which belongs to an equilibrium unit this course does not have. Just enough of it is taught here. |

## Not in this course

The four exams do not test these topics, so the book does not teach them. A class that also sits the AP Chemistry exam needs them from elsewhere.

| Topic | AP unit | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Composition: empirical and molecular formulas, percent composition, mass spectra of elements | Unit 1 |  |
| Gases: pressure, the ideal gas law, partial pressures, kinetic molecular theory | Unit 3 | Part 4 borrows two ideas from it (temperature as average kinetic energy, and the kelvin scale) and teaches them where they are needed. |
| Solutions and mixtures: chromatography, Beer’s law, colligative ideas | Unit 3 |  |
| Chemical equilibrium: K, Q, Le Châtelier’s principle | Unit 7 | Lesson 4.9 teaches the one piece the Final needs: a fast reversible step with equal forward and reverse rates. |
| Acids and bases: pH, weak-acid equilibria, buffers, titration curves | Unit 8 | Lesson 1.12 covers neutralization and simple titration only. |
| Thermodynamics: entropy and Gibbs free energy | Unit 9 |  |
| Electrochemistry: balancing redox by half-reactions, cells, cell potential | Unit 9 | Lesson 1.13 covers oxidation numbers and agents only. |

## How the absence of gaps is checked

`node tools/check.mjs` fails if any of these is untrue:

1. Every concept is defined in exactly one lesson.
2. Every concept a lesson builds on is taught in an earlier lesson, or is on the short list of assumed mathematics.
3. Every exam item is claimed by a lesson, and every concept the item depends on is taught before that exam and no later than the lesson that claims it.
4. Every lesson has all its parts, and every numerical answer in a worked example or practice question is recomputed from the question's data.
5. No lesson's text uses a glossary term before the lesson that defines it, unless it says where the term is defined.

The check cannot judge whether an explanation is good, only whether the order is sound. The concept lists for exam items are a reading of the exams and are open to revision in `src/data/exams.js`.
